cards.text: The LORD is still speaking to Moses, Israel's leader, right after warning Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan (Leviticus 18:3). Now He tells Moses to speak to the whole congregation of Israel. And He opens with a BIG one, no warm-up, no small talk: be holy.

cards.question: God tells the whole congregation of Israel to be holy. What reason does He give?

answers.text: Because the LORD their God is holy
Because the nations are watching them
Because they are about to enter the land

cards.text: Then God brings it close to home with a command about respect, and right next to it He says keep My Sabbaths. He signs off with a line you'll hear so often in this sermon, you'll be saying it in your sleep: "I am the LORD your God."

cards.question: Starting close to home, who does God say each person in Israel must respect?
Right after that, God names something Israel must not turn to or make for themselves out of molten metal. What is it?

cards.text: Next, the peace offering, offered so they'll be accepted. It can be eaten the day it's sacrificed or the next day, and that's the whole window. Two days, friend. I sat in a junk drawer for YEARS, and this offering doesn't even get a weekend.

cards.question: So what must happen to whatever's left of the peace offering on the third day?

answers.text: It is left for the poor

cards.question: If someone eats the peace offering on the third day, God will still accept it.

cards.text: Nope. By day three it's tainted, and whoever eats it has profaned what is holy to the LORD and must be cut off from his people.

Now harvest time. God says don't reap to the very edges of the field or gather the gleanings, and don't strip the vineyard bare or pick up the fallen grapes. Friend, I have scraped every mixing bowl I ever met CLEAN with this mustache, so this one's a stretch for me.

cards.question: Who does God say the edges of the field and the fallen grapes are left for?

cards.text: The poor and the foreigner. The LORD writes them right into the harvest plan and signs it: "I am the LORD your God."
Now God turns to how His people treat each other: no stealing, no lying, no deceiving one another.

cards.question: Swearing falsely by God's name would ___ His name.
No defrauding or robbing a neighbor. And a hired hand's wages? How long can they be held back?

answers.text: Until the end of the week

cards.text: Not even overnight, friend, so no "the check's in the mail." Then God speaks up for the deaf and the blind.

cards.question: God says it's okay to put a stumbling block before the blind as long as they can't tell who did it.

cards.text: Nope. No cursing the deaf, no stumbling blocks for the blind, but fear your God. Then it's off to court, where God says you must not pervert justice.

cards.question: In court, God tells Israel to show the poor a little extra favor.

cards.text: No partiality to the poor, no favoritism to the rich, just judge your neighbor fairly. Then no endangering your neighbor's life and no spreading slander, and yes, friend, that covers the group chat with one person conveniently left out.

cards.question: God says not to harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. So what should someone do instead?

answers.text: Let it go and say nothing

cards.question: Why does God say to rebuke your neighbor directly?

answers.text: So you won't incur guilt over him
So he will owe you an apology
So it never goes before a judge

cards.text: Then God says no revenge and no grudges against any of your people. A shiny new stamper took my spot on the counter and I got slid into the junk drawer for years, and you know what I'd say to that stamper today? "Teach me your ways."

cards.question: No revenge and no grudges. So what does God call for instead?

answers.text: Keep your distance from your neighbor
Forgive your neighbor once a year

cards.text: Love your neighbor as yourself. Centuries later, Jesus quotes this very line and calls it the second commandment, right after loving God (Matthew 22:37-39).
Now God says keep My statutes, and He gets VERY specific: no crossbreeding two kinds of livestock, and no sowing a field with two kinds of seed.

cards.question: God says clothing made of two kinds of material is fine to wear.

cards.text: My apron is quietly checking its own tag right now. Then comes a hard case about a man who sleeps with a slave girl promised to another man: there's due punishment but no death, since she hadn't been freed, and he brings a ram as a guilt offering and is forgiven.
When they enter the land and plant fruit trees, the fruit is forbidden for three years. THREE YEARS, friend, and I can't wait five minutes for a batch to cool.

cards.question: In the fourth year, what happens to all the fruit from those trees?

answers.text: It's consecrated as a praise offering
It is left for the poor and foreigner
It is sold to buy new seed

cards.text: And in the fifth year? They can finally EAT it. Five years, friend. The only thing I ever waited that long for was a drawer to open.

cards.question: God says following this plan for the fruit trees will increase their harvest.

cards.text: Then comes a quick run of don'ts: no eating anything with blood still in it, no divination or sorcery, no cuts for the dead or tattoos, no making a daughter a prostitute, and no clipping the edges of the beard. This mustache isn't a beard, but it still sat up straight.
Then that line again: keep My Sabbaths, and now reverence for His sanctuary too. And God warns them not to turn to mediums or spiritists.

cards.question: What does God say happens to people who seek out mediums and spiritists?

answers.text: They will be defiled by them
They will owe the priest a fine

cards.question: Next God turns to the elderly. What does He tell Israel to do in their presence?

answers.text: Wait for them to speak first

cards.question: When a foreigner lives in their land, God says don't oppress him. So how should Israel treat him?

answers.text: As native-born and loved as themselves
As a guest for one season only
As a hired hand on lower wages

cards.question: What reason does God give for loving the foreigner like that?

cards.text: On top of not oppressing the foreigner, love him as yourself, because they were foreigners in Egypt once. Then God heads to the market: no dishonest measures of length, weight or volume, so no "one cup" that's secretly three-quarters, not in Israel and not in my bakery.

cards.question: God wants honest ___ and weights, plus an honest ephah and an honest hin.

cards.text: He signs that one: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." Then He closes it all with keep all My statutes and all My ordinances and follow them, and that's where we'll leave it for now, friend, so keep that apron on, because God isn't done teaching His people to be holy.

findings.problem: Multiple choice takes five of the six choice cards in stop 1 (cards 2, 4, 5, 7, 11). The only other type is one true or false (card 8), and there is no fill in the blank.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: 'Next, the peace offering...', 'It can be eaten...', 'Two days, friend.' and 'I sat in a junk drawer...'.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke says the offering 'doesn't even get a weekend', but the eating window is two days, which is the length of a weekend. The comparison works against the punchline instead of landing.

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'Now harvest time.', the gleaning rules and the mixing bowl joke.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card opens by repeating card 11's answer ('The poor and the foreigner.') and then restates it as the harvest plan. The only new content is the 'I am the LORD your God' line, so the card mostly recaps instead of moving the passage forward.

This story card has three sentences ('Nope.', the deaf and blind line, and the court line). It also carries more than two things: cursing the deaf, stumbling blocks for the blind, fear your God, and perverting justice.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: This story card carries three things: judging fairly without partiality, not endangering a neighbor's life, and not spreading slander, plus the group chat joke.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The question asks what to do 'instead' of harboring hatred. Leviticus 19:17 puts the two commands side by side and doesn't say one replaces the other. Verse 18 has 'but'; verse 17 has no such word.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This story card puts the mixed fabric joke for 19:19 together with the whole slave girl case from 19:20-22. That case alone holds several beats: the act, due punishment, no death because she wasn't freed, the ram, and forgiveness.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The right answer is the only one with a contraction ('It's'), while both wrong answers start with 'It is'. It is also the only one in Bible wording ('consecrated as a praise offering'), so it stands out from the others.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: 'And in the fifth year?', 'They can finally EAT it.', 'Five years, friend.' and the drawer joke.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke 'The only thing I ever waited that long for was a drawer to open' suggests the drawer stayed closed for years. That changes his backstory, where the drawer opened often for scissors or tape and everyone held their breath each time.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: 'Five years, friend' stretches the wait. The fruit is forbidden for three years, offered in the fourth, and eaten in the fifth year (Leviticus 19:23-25), so the wait isn't a full five years.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: This summary card for the 19:26-29 stretch lists every rule one by one (blood, divination, sorcery, cuts, tattoos, prostitution, beard) instead of saying in a few words what the stretch covers.

rule.text: He says in a few words what it covers and doesn't go item by item.

findings.problem: The first sentence repeats the answers to cards 12 and 13: don't oppress the foreigner, love him as yourself, because they were foreigners in Egypt.
The wrong answer 'promises' can be argued as right. Leviticus 19:11-12 forbids lying and swearing falsely, so God does want honest promises.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.
